title: An economic assessment of the World Health Organization's 75% tobacco tax incidence target
gist: Oxford Economics finds the WHO's recommendation that taxes make up at least 75% of cigarette retail prices is met by only 39 of 178 countries (2024) and is a weak policy benchmark: per-pack tax correlates 91% with retail prices versus 49% for tax incidence, and incidence relates weakly to affordability and smoking prevalence. It argues for country-specific tobacco tax policy instead of a single global incidence target.

insights.claim: The World Health Organization recommends that taxes account for at least 75% of the retail price of cigarettes, a benchmark Oxford Economics assessed for origins, application and economic evidence.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Defines the policy benchmark that drives excise-hike pressure on tobacco markets globally.

insights.claim: In 2024 only 39 of 178 countries in the WHO dataset met the 75% tobacco tax incidence threshold, with compliant countries concentrated disproportionately among high-income and EU economies.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Most markets, especially emerging ones, sit below the target, implying latent excise-increase risk for tobacco volumes there if WHO pressure succeeds.

themes.theme: Tax incidence is a weak policy lever

insights.claim: Tobacco tax incidence (tax as a share of retail price) is driven partly by factors outside governments' direct control, including producer and retailer pricing, product mix and consumer behaviour.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Manufacturer pricing power mechanically lowers incidence, so a high-incidence target can be pushed against by price increases rather than tax policy.

insights.claim: Across 174 countries in the 2024 WHO dataset, tax paid per pack correlates 91% with retail cigarette prices, versus only 49% for tax incidence and retail prices.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Absolute per-pack specific excise, not incidence ratios, is the better predictor of cigarette prices, relevant for modelling price and volume effects of tax changes.

insights.claim: Tax incidence shows relatively weak relationships with both cigarette affordability and smoking prevalence, undermining it as a public-health outcome metric.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Challenges the WHO benchmark's evidentiary basis, supporting industry and fiscal arguments against incidence-based excise hikes.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics concludes tobacco tax policy should reflect country differences in income levels, market structures, consumer behaviour, illicit trade, tax administration and wider fiscal and public-health objectives rather than a single global tax-incidence target.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Points to heterogeneous, country-by-country excise paths; illicit-trade and fiscal-revenue considerations may cap aggressive tax increases.
